Writing Music Down: Choosing the Right Notation

There is no single right way to write music down. A notation is a tool. Each one shows some things clearly and leaves others out, and each belongs to a tradition whose players read it fluently. This lesson writes one melody six ways so you can compare them side by side, then says when to reach for each.

The melody is the opening of Mò Lì Huā (茉莉花, Jasmine Flower), a Chinese folk song known across the world. It uses only five notes (a pentatonic scale), which also exists in Indian music: Hindustani musicians call that scale rāg Bhūpālī and Carnatic musicians rāga Mōhanam. So it can be written naturally in every system on this page.

Every example below is this same phrase.

NoteIB: why notation choice matters in MYP and DP

In both programmes, how you show music is part of how you show understanding. Examiners and teachers look for notation that is appropriate to the music and used accurately. Writing a Chinese folk song only in staff notation, or a beat made in a DAW only as a waveform picture, can hide exactly the things you need to discuss. The notes in the boxes below say what to watch for in each programme. Always check the current subject guide and your teacher’s instructions: the details of assessment change between guide editions.

The six notations at a glance

Notation Shows well Leaves out or blurs Typical home
Staff (Western) notation exact pitch and rhythm, harmony, several parts at once tuning between the 12 notes, ornaments of other traditions, timbre Western classical, jazz, film, band, most published music
Jianpu (numbered notation) scale degrees, rhythm, lyrics; quick to write and to transpose harmony and multiple parts are clumsy Chinese folk, pop and instrumental music; also Indonesia, Japan
Sargam (Hindustani and Carnatic) scale degrees in a rāga, rhythm against the tāla cycle the ornaments (gamaka, mīnd) that matter most; it’s a memory aid, not a full score Indian classical teaching and composition
DAW screenshot (piano roll, arrangement) exact timing, velocity, structure, layers, effects and automation key, harmony and musical meaning; it is a picture of data, not something to read electronic, pop production, any music made in a computer
Waveform loudness over time, where sounds start, silence, clipping pitch, harmony, almost everything else editing audio, checking timing and dynamics
Spectrogram which frequencies sound when: timbre, harmonics, vibrato it’s hard to read notes, rhythm or harmony from it, especially with several instruments acoustics, voice, sound design, analysis of non-pitched music

Staff notation

Five lines, notes placed on lines and spaces for pitch, note shapes for length. Its strengths: exact pitch (every one of the 12 notes in every octave), exact rhythm, and many parts at once lined up vertically, so harmony and counterpoint can be seen. That’s why orchestral, choral and band music, and almost all analysis of Western harmony, uses it.

Its weaknesses: it assumes the 12 equal notes of a piano, so pitches between them (blue notes, Arabic maqām, Indian shruti, the slides of Chinese erhu playing) need extra signs or prose. It also needs training to read quickly.

Use it when: writing for Western instruments or ensembles; analysing harmony, voice leading or form in Western music; when exact rhythm and pitch must be communicated to a reader who will play it.

NoteMYP and DP notes: staff notation
  • MYP: you don’t have to use staff notation in MYP Music, but when you analyse Western music, short notated examples (a motif, a chord progression) are the clearest evidence. Label what you’re showing: circle the motif and name it, write the chord symbols above. In your process journal, a scan of a hand-written sketch is fine.
  • DP: when you discuss a Western work in the Exploring music in context portfolio or an analysis, quote short, annotated excerpts with bar numbers instead of long unmarked pages, and say where they come from. For your own compositions, staff notation is expected where the music is written for performers to read; use notation software and check that what is written matches what you intend to be played.

Jianpu (numbered notation)

Jianpu (简谱, “simplified notation”) numbers the notes of the scale: 1 to 7 are do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. The key is given at the start (1 = F means do is F). A dot above a number puts it an octave up, a dot below an octave down. A plain number lasts one beat; each line under a number halves it; a dash after it adds a beat. Bar lines are as in staff notation.

It was spread in China in the early 20th century from a French numbered system, and is still how most Chinese musicians write and read folk songs, pop songs and parts for traditional instruments like the erhu, pipa and dizi. Because it writes scale degrees, not fixed pitches, the same page can be played in any key just by changing “1 =”.

Use it when: writing or studying Chinese music, or when the players read jianpu; writing a single melody with lyrics quickly; teaching melodies by scale degree (it pairs naturally with tonal solfège).

NoteMYP and DP notes: jianpu
  • MYP: if you investigate a Chinese musical tradition (Criterion A, Investigating), showing the music in jianpu, with a short key that explains the dots, lines and dashes, demonstrates that you understand how the tradition itself writes music. Put staff notation next to it if your reader won’t know jianpu.
  • DP: in the portfolio or an analysis, quoting music from a Chinese tradition in its own notation is a sign of working in context. Provide a legend the first time, and if you compare it with a Western piece, a parallel staff version helps the examiner follow. Don’t just transcribe it into staff notation and leave the original out.

Sargam: Hindustani and Carnatic notation

Indian classical music names the notes of the scale Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni (sargam), shortened to their first letters. Sa is the home note, chosen by the singer; like jianpu, it writes scale degrees, not fixed pitches. The two classical traditions write it a little differently.

Hindustani (North Indian): Bhatkhande notation

Developed by Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande in the early 20th century. Each box is one mātrā (beat). Notes sharing a beat are joined by a curve beneath. A dot above a note is the upper octave (Ṡ), a dot below is the lower. A dash holds the previous note (some books use the Devanagari sign ऽ instead). Underneath, the tāla (the rhythmic cycle) is marked: X is sam, the first and strongest beat, and 0 is khālī, the “empty” beat. This melody fits exactly one cycle of the eight-beat Keherwā tāla. A flat (komal) note is shown by a line under it, and the raised Ma (tīvra) by a line above.

Carnatic (South Indian): swara notation

Carnatic notation writes the swaras in lower-case letters (s r g m p d n), with dots for octaves, a comma to extend a note by one time unit and a semicolon for two. The tāla is marked with bar lines at the end of each section: one line after the laghu (four beats here) and after each drutam (two beats), and a double line at the end of the cycle. Eight beats is Ādi tāla, the most common Carnatic tāla, so this melody fills exactly one cycle of it too.

What sargam leaves out

The most important part of a rāga is how notes are approached: slides (mīnd), oscillations (gamaka), which notes are lingered on. The written swaras give the skeleton only, and students learn the rest by ear from a teacher. Many pieces are never written at all. So sargam notation is a reliable memory aid and teaching tool, not a complete score.

Use it when: studying, teaching or composing in an Indian tradition; showing the shape of a rāga; showing how a melody sits against a tāla cycle.

NoteMYP and DP notes: sargam
  • MYP: in an investigation of Indian music, use the tradition’s own terms (rāga, tāla, sam, khālī, swara) and its notation for short examples. Explain in your own words what the notation cannot show, such as gamaka, and support it with a timestamped recording (“listen at 1:42 for the slide from Ga to Re”).
  • DP: for the portfolio or an analysis of Indian music, sargam with a legend, plus precise timestamps in a named recording, is stronger evidence than a staff transcription alone. Staff notation can’t show the shruti and gamaka you’d be discussing. If you do transcribe to staff for comparison, say what it loses. Name the tradition (Hindustani or Carnatic), and the rāga and tāla.

DAW screenshots

A digital audio workstation (DAW) shows music the way the computer stores it. The piano roll (top) is a grid: time runs left to right, pitch bottom to top, each bar is a note, and its shade is how hard it is played (velocity). The arrangement view (bottom) shows every track as a lane of blocks (regions or clips), with lines for automation: a volume fade, a filter opening.

What it’s good at: exact timing and velocity, how a track is layered and structured, which sounds, effects and automation were used. For electronic music, hip hop and most pop production, this is the score: the music was never written any other way.

What it’s bad at: it doesn’t tell the reader the key, the chords or the beat they should feel. It’s a picture to be explained, not something a performer can read. A wall of tiny clips means nothing without labels.

Use it when: the music was made in a DAW; showing production decisions (layers, effects, automation, edits); showing a process (before and after).

NoteMYP and DP notes: DAW screenshots
  • MYP: screenshots are excellent process-journal evidence for Criterion B (Developing) and C (Creating): show a “before” and “after” with a sentence on why you changed it. Crop to what matters, zoom so it’s readable, and add arrows and labels. A full-screen screenshot of the whole project with no annotation shows very little.
  • DP: in the Experimenting with music report and in production-based Presenting music or HL project work, annotated DAW screenshots are often the most appropriate evidence for music created in a DAW. Annotate them: name the track, the plug-in and the setting, and say what musical effect it had. Pair a screenshot with a timestamp in the audio (“the filter opens at 0:48”). For anything that will be performed by players, include a readable score or lead sheet as well.

Waveforms

A waveform draws the sound itself: how far the speaker cone moves, over time. Zoomed out (top), it shows loudness over time: where notes start, how they fade, where the silences are, and whether the recording is clipping (flat-topped at the edges). Zoomed right in (bottom), you can see individual cycles of the wave (see Sound 1).

That’s about all it shows. You cannot read the pitches, the harmony or the instruments from it.

Use it when: showing where an edit, an entry or a hit happens; comparing the dynamics of two performances or two masters; showing that a recording is too quiet or distorted.

Spectrograms

A spectrogram shows time left to right, frequency bottom to top, and loudness as brightness. Each note appears as a stack of lines (its harmonics), so it shows timbre, vibrato and which frequencies are present when. Here you can see the melody’s notes, each with its harmonics above, and the slight vibrato on the long notes.

With one clean instrument, it can be surprisingly readable. With a full band it becomes a dense cloud from which notes, chords and rhythm are very hard to pick out. Specialists use it for voice (formants), acoustics, birdsong, and for music where pitch isn’t the point: electronic textures, noise music, extended techniques.

Use it when: your point is about timbre, a sound’s frequency content, vibrato or a texture with no clear notes, and only with labels that point at what to look at.

NoteMYP and DP notes: waveforms and spectrograms
  • MYP and DP alike: use them only when they show the point you’re making (dynamics, timing, timbre), and say what to look at. A waveform or spectrogram dropped in as decoration isn’t evidence of anything, and it won’t stand in for notation. One cropped, labelled image with a timestamp beats a full-track screenshot.
  • DP: in an analysis of electronic or non-notated music, a spectrogram with a labelled feature (“the sweep from 200 Hz to 5 kHz is the filter opening”) can support a point about timbre or production that no score could show. Keep it as support for your writing, not a substitute.

Choosing: a short checklist

  1. Whose music is it? Use the notation the tradition itself uses (staff for a Bach chorale, jianpu for a Chinese folk song, sargam for a bandish, a DAW view for a track made in Ableton), and add a translation only if your reader needs it.
  2. What’s the point you’re making? Harmony → staff. Scale degrees and melody → jianpu or sargam. Production → DAW. Dynamics or timing of a recording → waveform. Timbre → spectrogram.
  3. Who has to read it? A performer needs something playable. An examiner needs something labelled.
  4. What does it leave out? Say so, and fill the gap with a recording and a timestamp.
  5. Crop, label, cite. Short excerpts, bar numbers or timestamps, the source of every example.
NoteMYP and DP notes: presenting evidence in general
  • Legends. The first time you use any notation your reader might not know (jianpu, sargam, a graphic score), give a two-line key.
  • Accuracy. Wrong notes or rhythms in a notated example undermine the point it makes. Check every example against the recording.
  • Citations. Every quoted score, recording and screenshot of someone else’s work needs a source.
  • Recordings and timestamps. For music that isn’t primarily written down, the recording is the primary source, and a timestamp is your “bar number”.
  • Your own work. In both programmes, evidence of process (sketches, screenshots of versions, short recordings of tries) counts. Date it and say what changed.
